unitPlan.title: Éveil du printemps
unitPlan.bigIdeas: Observer les changements de printemps dans l'environnement et comprendre le réveil de la nature

lessons.title: Le printemps arrive - premiers signes
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe and identify the first signs that spring is beginning in our environment

decisionPoints.question: What early spring signs are visible around our school today?
decisionPoints.guidance: If many signs visible: Focus on detailed observation of 3-4 signs. If few signs: Use photos to supplement and discuss what to look for.

decisionPoints.question: Should we start with temperature observations or outdoor exploration?
decisionPoints.guidance: If weather mild: Start with outdoor spring hunt. If still cold: Begin indoors with temperature comparison to winter.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready to compare winter and spring conditions?
decisionPoints.guidance: If engaged: Create simple comparison chart. If overwhelmed: Focus on one spring sign at a time.

lessons.opening: Circle time (8 min): Show winter photo of school yard from earlier this year. Ask 'Qu'est-ce qui est différent maintenant?' Look out window together. Point and name: 'C'est le printemps!' Teach spring gesture (arms opening like flowers).
lessons.mainActivity: Spring detective walk (27 min): Outdoor exploration with clipboards and spring signs checklist. Students search for: warmer air (feel with hands), longer daylight (discuss morning/evening), buds on trees, birds singing, people wearing lighter clothes. Each student draws 2-3 spring signs they find. Practice saying 'Au printemps, je vois...' Create class spring discovery chart with student findings.
lessons.closing: Science circle (10 min): Students share one spring sign they discovered. Teacher records on class chart with simple drawings. End with spring awakening chant: 'Le printemps arrive, tout se réveille!'
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If students get distracted outside: Use 'spring scientist' focus signal. If too many observations: Choose 2-3 main signs to focus on. If weather turns bad: Adapt to window observations with binoculars.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students recognize spring changes they see walking to school or playing outside with families
lessons.visualSupports: Spring signs checklist with pictures, hand gestures for warmth (spreading arms), seasonal comparison photos, spring vocabulary cards

lessons.title: Les bourgeons réveillent
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe buds on trees and understand that plants are waking up from winter rest

decisionPoints.question: Which trees show the clearest bud development in our area?
decisionPoints.guidance: If obvious buds available: Take students to examine closely. If buds hard to see: Bring branch samples indoors for closer inspection.

decisionPoints.question: Should we examine buds up close or observe from a distance first?
decisionPoints.guidance: If students focused: Use magnifying glasses for detailed bud examination. If restless: Start with pointing and naming from distance.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for before-and-after bud comparison activities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If understanding developing: Compare winter branch photo to current buds. If confused: Focus on simple bud identification first.

lessons.opening: Connection to previous lesson (8 min): Review spring signs from Lesson 1. Today we're looking closer at trees. Show sleeping gesture: 'En hiver, les arbres dorment.' Then waking up gesture: 'Au printemps, ils se réveillent!' Introduce 'bourgeons' with hand motions.
lessons.mainActivity: Tree awakening exploration (27 min): Outdoor investigation focusing on tree branches and buds. Students work in pairs to find different types of buds using observation sheets. Use magnifying glasses to examine bud shapes, colors, and sizes. Practice vocabulary: 'Je vois des bourgeons sur les branches.' Students draw their favorite buds and predict what will happen next. Create class bud observation journal with student drawings and predictions.
lessons.closing: Bud discovery sharing (10 min): Students show their bud drawings and share predictions. Teacher introduces concept: 'Les bourgeons vont devenir des feuilles!' End with tree awakening movement: arms as branches, hands as buds slowly opening.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If magnifying glasses get lost: Focus on pointing and naming visible buds. If students pick buds: Explain 'look but don't touch' rule for plant health. If no obvious buds: Use prepared branch samples.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students notice buds on trees in their neighborhoods and understand trees are getting ready to grow
lessons.visualSupports: Bud identification cards with pictures, sleeping/waking gestures, magnifying glass demonstration, tree awakening movements

lessons.title: Pourquoi les plantes se réveillent-elles?
lessons.oneGoal: Students will understand that plants wake up in spring because they get more sun and warmth

decisionPoints.question: How can we make sun and warmth needs concrete for young learners?
decisionPoints.guidance: If sunny day: Go outside to feel warmth directly on skin. If cloudy: Use lamp and thermometer to demonstrate warmth concept.

decisionPoints.question: Should we use plant growth experiments or simple demonstrations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If students engaged with hands-on: Start simple germination experiment. If need more concrete: Use dramatic play with sun and plant roles.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for basic cause-and-effect discussions about plant needs?
decisionPoints.guidance: If making connections: Discuss sun → warmth → plant growth. If struggling: Focus on simple observation of warm/cold plant responses.

lessons.opening: Connecting to buds (8 min): Review buds from Lesson 2. Ask 'Pourquoi les bourgeons se réveillent maintenant?' Introduce sun and warmth concepts with gestures: sun rays (arms spreading), warmth (hugging self), plant growth (growing taller).
lessons.mainActivity: Plant needs investigation (27 min): Dramatic exploration of plant needs using movement and props. Students act as sleeping plants (curled up), then teacher adds 'sun' (flashlight) and 'warmth' (warm air from heater), and plants 'wake up' and grow. Set up simple experiment: place identical plants in warm sunny spot vs. cool dark spot. Students predict what will happen. Create plant needs chart with drawings of sun, warmth, and growing plants. Practice saying 'Les plantes ont besoin de soleil et de chaleur.'
lessons.closing: Plant needs review (10 min): Students demonstrate plant awakening sequence with movements. Review plant needs chart together. End with plant awakening song: 'Soleil, chaleur, les plantes poussent!'
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If plants not available: Use seeds or pictures for demonstration. If weather too cold for outdoor warmth sensing: Use indoor warm/cool comparison. If students get silly during drama: Redirect with 'serious scientist' signal.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand why their family gardens start growing when weather gets warmer in spring
lessons.visualSupports: Sun and warmth gesture cards, plant growth sequence pictures, before/after plant photos, plant needs chart with symbols

lessons.title: Les premières feuilles vertes
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe the emergence of new green leaves and understand this shows healthy plant growth

decisionPoints.question: Which plants show the most obvious new leaf growth?
decisionPoints.guidance: If clear examples available outdoors: Focus on bushes and trees with visible new growth. If limited examples: Bring in fast-growing plant samples.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on one type of plant or compare multiple species?
decisionPoints.guidance: If students engaged: Compare leaf shapes and sizes on different plants. If overwhelmed: Focus on one clear example with obvious new leaves.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for leaf shape and size observation activities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If detailed observation skills developing: Use leaf templates for tracing and comparison. If need simpler activity: Focus on green color identification and counting leaves.

lessons.opening: Building on plant growth (8 min): Review how sun and warmth help plants grow from Lesson 3. Today we'll see what happens to buds! Show sequence: bud → small leaf → bigger leaf. Use hand gestures to show leaf unfurling from closed fist to open hand.
lessons.mainActivity: New leaf discovery walk (27 min): Outdoor leaf investigation focusing on brand-new spring growth. Students search for the tiniest new leaves and the brightest green colors. Use simple leaf observation sheets to draw different leaf shapes and sizes. Count new leaves on chosen branches. Practice vocabulary: 'Je vois de nouvelles feuilles vertes.' Compare new spring leaves with old ones still on trees. Create class leaf collection (draw, don't pick) showing variety of new spring growth.
lessons.closing: Leaf growth celebration (10 min): Students share their favorite new leaf discoveries. Discuss how new leaves show plants are healthy and growing. End with leaf growing movement: start as tiny buds, slowly unfurl into full leaves reaching toward the sun.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If students want to pick leaves: Explain leaves help plants breathe and eat. If new growth hard to find: Use potted plants with obvious new growth. If attention wanders: Make it a 'green hunt' game.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students notice new green leaves appearing on trees and plants around their homes and playgrounds
lessons.visualSupports: Leaf growth sequence cards, leaf shape templates, color identification chart, hand gestures for leaf unfurling

lessons.title: Il fait plus chaud - mesurer le printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe that spring brings warmer temperatures and learn to measure temperature changes

decisionPoints.question: What temperature measuring tools work best for Grade 1 students?
decisionPoints.guidance: If large outdoor thermometer available: Use for whole-class reading. If only small thermometers: Work in small groups with adult support.

decisionPoints.question: Should we compare morning and afternoon temperatures?
decisionPoints.guidance: If full day available: Take readings at different times. If single lesson: Compare indoor/outdoor or sunny/shady temperatures.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for simple temperature recording activities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If number concepts solid: Record actual numbers on chart. If numbers challenging: Use simple warmer/cooler comparisons with pictures.

lessons.opening: Connection to warmth (8 min): Review how plants need warmth from Lesson 3. Ask students to feel the air temperature with their skin. Introduce thermometer as a tool that 'tells us how warm or cold it is.' Show thermometer and demonstrate reading it together.
lessons.mainActivity: Temperature investigation (27 min): Outdoor temperature exploration using classroom thermometer. Students take turns reading the thermometer in different locations: sunny spots, shady areas, near building, in open space. Record temperatures on simple chart using pictures (sun for warm, snowflake for cold). Practice vocabulary: 'Il fait plus chaud aujourd'hui.' Compare current spring temperature to winter temperature from earlier in year. Students draw pictures showing how temperature affects their clothing choices and activities.
lessons.closing: Temperature discoveries (10 min): Review temperature findings from different locations. Discuss why some spots are warmer than others. End with temperature movement: huddle together for cold, spread out with arms up for warm.
materials: Winter temperature comparison data if available
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If thermometer breaks: Use body temperature sensing (hands in different locations). If numbers too difficult: Focus on warmer/cooler concepts with gestures. If weather suddenly changes: Use as learning opportunity about spring weather variability.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand how families check weather temperature to decide what clothes to wear
lessons.visualSupports: Large thermometer with clear numbers, temperature comparison chart with pictures, warm/cold gesture cards, clothing choice visuals

lessons.title: Les jours deviennent plus longs
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe that daylight hours increase in spring and understand how this affects living things

decisionPoints.question: How can we make daylight changes visible to young students?
decisionPoints.guidance: If clear morning/evening reference points: Compare when it gets dark now vs. winter. If abstract: Use clock and window light demonstrations.

decisionPoints.question: Should we track sunrise/sunset times or use classroom observations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If family support available: Send home simple observation sheet. If classroom-only: Focus on school day light changes.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for before-and-after daylight comparisons?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comparison skills developing: Use photos of same location in winter vs. spring. If need concrete: Focus on current light observations only.

lessons.opening: Building on temperature (8 min): Review warmer spring temperatures from Lesson 5. Introduce new concept: spring days are also longer! Ask students if they notice staying up later or getting up when it's lighter. Show window and discuss how much light we see.
lessons.mainActivity: Daylight exploration (27 min): Indoor and outdoor investigation of daily light changes. Students observe light coming through classroom windows at different times if possible. Go outside to notice how bright it is and compare to students' memories of winter darkness. Create simple timeline showing winter short days vs. spring longer days using pictures. Practice vocabulary: 'Les jours sont plus longs au printemps.' Discuss how longer light affects plants (more growing time) and animals (more time to find food and be active).
lessons.closing: Long day celebration (10 min): Students share what they like about longer spring days. Create class list of spring day activities that weren't possible in short winter days. End with day length movement: short winter day (small, curled up) growing into long spring day (arms stretched wide).
materials: Pictures of winter vs. spring daylight
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If daylight changes hard to visualize: Use flashlight to show short vs. long light periods. If students get restless: Make it active with movement representing day length. If too abstract: Focus on concrete 'we can play outside later' examples.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students recognize they can play outside later and families don't turn lights on as early
lessons.visualSupports: Day length comparison pictures, clock faces showing daylight hours, before/after photos of same location, timeline with sun symbols

lessons.title: Les animaux se réveillent aussi
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe how animals become more active in spring as they emerge from winter rest

decisionPoints.question: Which local animals show obvious spring activity increases?
decisionPoints.guidance: If birds visible: Focus on increased singing and movement. If insects emerging: Point out bees and butterflies. If mammals active: Discuss squirrels being more visible.

decisionPoints.question: Should we observe real animals or use photos and videos?
decisionPoints.guidance: If animals easily observable outdoors: Conduct live animal observation. If limited wildlife: Supplement with videos of local spring animal behavior.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for animal behavior prediction activities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If making connections: Have students predict what animals will do in spring warmth. If need concrete: Focus on simple observation and description first.

lessons.opening: Connecting to longer days (8 min): Review longer spring days from Lesson 6. Introduce new idea: animals also notice spring changes! Ask students if they've seen more birds, insects, or other animals lately. Use movement to show sleepy winter animals waking up.
lessons.mainActivity: Spring animal observation (27 min): Outdoor animal activity investigation. Students work in pairs to observe and record animal signs: bird sounds, insect movements, animal tracks, evidence of animal activity. Use simple animal observation sheets with pictures to identify common spring animals. Practice vocabulary: 'Les animaux sont plus actifs.' Create class animal activity chart showing what animals do differently in spring vs. winter. Discuss why animals are more active (warmer weather, more food, longer days).
lessons.closing: Animal awakening sharing (10 min): Students demonstrate animal movements they observed or imagined. Share findings from animal activity chart. End with animal awakening sequence: hibernate (sleep), feel warmth (stretch), become active (move around).
materials: Animal observation sheets with local species
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If few animals visible: Use recorded bird sounds and discuss what animals are doing even if we can't see them. If students get too excited: Use quiet observation signals. If weather interferes: Observe from windows and discuss what we might see.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students notice more birds singing, bees buzzing, and animals moving around their neighborhoods
lessons.visualSupports: Local animal identification cards, animal movement gestures, before/after seasonal behavior pictures, simple tracking sheets

lessons.title: Les oiseaux construisent des nids
lessons.oneGoal: Students will understand that spring is nesting season and observe bird nest-building behaviors

decisionPoints.question: Which nesting birds can students safely observe in our area?
decisionPoints.guidance: If nests visible from distance: Use binoculars for observation without disturbing. If no visible nests: Use videos or pictures of local nesting birds.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on nest materials or nest locations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If students engaged with details: Examine twigs, grass, and other nest materials on ground. If overwhelmed: Focus on simple concept that birds make homes.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for simple bird behavior observation activities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If observation skills strong: Watch for birds carrying materials or sitting on nests. If need structure: Use checklist of nesting behaviors to look for.

lessons.opening: Building on animal activity (8 min): Review how animals are more active in spring from Lesson 7. Focus on birds today. Ask if students have noticed birds carrying sticks or grass. Introduce concept: birds build nests in spring! Use hand motions to show building/weaving actions.
lessons.mainActivity: Bird nesting investigation (27 min): Outdoor bird and nest observation focusing on nesting behaviors and materials. Students look for: birds carrying materials, existing nests in trees (from safe distance), nest-building materials on ground. Use bird behavior observation sheets to record what they see. Practice vocabulary: 'Les oiseaux construisent des nids.' Collect fallen nest materials (twigs, grass, feathers) to examine how birds build homes. Create classroom display of nest materials and discuss why birds choose different materials.
lessons.closing: Nest building understanding (10 min): Students examine collected nest materials and discuss how birds use them. Share observations of bird behaviors. End with bird nest building movements: gathering materials (picking up), carrying (walking with arms full), building (weaving motions).
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If no nesting activity visible: Use prepared nest materials and discuss how birds would use them. If students disturb wildlife: Review observation-only rules. If materials get mixed up: Focus on main types (twigs, grass, soft materials).
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand why they see birds carrying sticks and building nests in trees around their homes
lessons.visualSupports: Bird nesting behavior cards, nest material identification guide, building motion demonstrations, seasonal nesting timeline

lessons.title: Pourquoi faire des nids au printemps?
lessons.oneGoal: Students will understand that animals make nests in spring to prepare for their babies

decisionPoints.question: How can we explain animal reproduction appropriately for Grade 1?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comfortable discussing: Focus on baby animals needing safe homes. If sensitive topic: Emphasize protection and care concepts only.

decisionPoints.question: Should we use nest examples or focus on animal family concepts?
decisionPoints.guidance: If concrete examples available: Show how nests protect babies. If abstract: Compare to human homes keeping families safe.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for discussions about animal care and protection?
decisionPoints.guidance: If understanding developing: Discuss how parents (animal and human) protect their young. If need simpler: Focus on nests as safe, warm homes.

lessons.opening: Connecting to nest building (8 min): Review bird nest building from Lesson 8. Ask students why they think birds work so hard to build nests. Introduce concept: nests are homes for baby birds! Use caring gestures to show protection and safety.
lessons.mainActivity: Animal family exploration (27 min): Investigation of how animals prepare homes for babies using pictures, videos, and discussion. Students look at photos of baby birds in nests, discuss why babies need protection. Compare animal families to human families - both need safe homes. Practice vocabulary: 'Les parents protègent leurs bébés.' Create class book about animal families showing different animals and their babies in spring homes. Students draw pictures of animal families being safe and cared for.
lessons.closing: Family care understanding (10 min): Students share their animal family drawings and explain how parents take care of babies. Review why spring is good time for animal babies (warm weather, lots of food). End with family care movements: building safe home, feeding babies, keeping them warm.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If students ask detailed reproduction questions: Redirect to homes and care focus. If some students lack family reference: Include diverse family structures in discussion. If emotional responses: Emphasize safety and love concepts.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand that both animal families and human families work to keep their babies safe and cared for
lessons.visualSupports: Animal family photo cards, baby animal pictures, family care gesture cards, diverse family structure examples

lessons.title: Expérience: faire pousser des graines
lessons.oneGoal: Students will conduct experiments to grow seeds and understand how plants begin life in spring

decisionPoints.question: Which seeds are most appropriate for quick classroom germination?
decisionPoints.guidance: If fast results desired: Use bean or sunflower seeds for quick sprouting. If longer timeline acceptable: Try flower seeds that relate to spring themes.

decisionPoints.question: Should we plant seeds individually or in groups?
decisionPoints.guidance: If students need ownership: Individual small pots for each student. If classroom management easier: Small groups sharing larger containers.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for daily observation and recording activities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If routine established: Daily seed growth journal with drawings. If need simpler: Weekly observations with teacher-guided recording.

lessons.opening: Connecting to plant growth (8 min): Review how plants need sun and warmth from earlier lessons. Introduce new concept: plants start from tiny seeds! Show various seeds and ask students to predict what they might grow into.
lessons.mainActivity: Seed planting experiment (27 min): Hands-on seed planting investigation where students plant seeds and set up growth experiment. Each student plants 2-3 seeds in small pots with soil and water. Set up controlled experiment: some seeds with water, some without; some in light, some in dark. Students make predictions about which seeds will grow best. Practice vocabulary: 'Je plante des graines dans la terre.' Create seed growth tracking charts where students will draw daily observations. Discuss what seeds need to grow (water, soil, warmth, light).
lessons.closing: Seed experiment setup (10 min): Students explain their predictions about which seeds will grow best. Review what seeds need to grow. End with seed growth movement: start curled up like seed, slowly grow with water and sun until tall plant.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If seeds don't germinate: Have backup sprouted seeds ready. If soil gets messy: Have cleanup supplies ready and assign helpers. If watering is uneven: Teach careful watering technique or control watering yourself.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand how gardens and farms start with tiny seeds that grow into food and flowers
lessons.visualSupports: Seed identification cards, plant growth sequence pictures, planting step-by-step guide, growth tracking templates

lessons.title: Les fleurs apparaissent
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe spring flowers and understand they help plants make new seeds

decisionPoints.question: Which spring flowers are safest and most accessible for observation?
decisionPoints.guidance: If school garden available: Focus on daffodils, tulips, or other safe spring blooms. If limited flowers: Bring in cut flowers for close examination.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on flower colors, shapes, or scents first?
decisionPoints.guidance: If students engaged with details: Explore colors, shapes, and smells systematically. If need simpler: Focus on color identification and beauty appreciation.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for discussions about why flowers are colorful?
decisionPoints.guidance: If making connections: Introduce concept that bright colors attract insects. If abstract: Focus on observation and description first.

lessons.opening: Building on plant growth (8 min): Check seed experiment from Lesson 10 and celebrate any sprouting. Introduce today's focus: flowers are appearing on plants outside! Ask students what flowers they've noticed. Show examples of spring flowers.
lessons.mainActivity: Spring flower investigation (27 min): Outdoor flower observation and exploration focusing on spring blooms. Students use flower observation sheets to record colors, shapes, sizes, and scents of different flowers. Practice vocabulary: 'Je vois des fleurs colorées.' Use magnifying glasses to examine flower parts up close. Students create flower color wheel showing all the spring flower colors they find. Discuss why flowers are colorful and smell nice (to attract insects). Gentle flower touching and smelling activities (with safe flowers only).
lessons.closing: Flower beauty celebration (10 min): Students share their favorite flower discoveries and explain why they liked them. Show flower color wheel and discuss variety of spring flowers. End with flower blooming movement: start as closed bud, slowly open into beautiful flower with arms as petals.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If allergies are concern: Keep flower observation visual only. If no flowers blooming yet: Use potted flowers or high-quality photos. If students pick flowers: Explain how flowers help plants and practice 'look don't take' rule.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students enjoy the beautiful flowers that bloom in gardens, parks, and wild areas during springtime
lessons.visualSupports: Spring flower identification cards, color wheel examples, flower parts diagrams, bloom sequence pictures

lessons.title: Les insectes reviennent
lessons.oneGoal: Students will observe that insects become active in spring and understand their connection to flowers

decisionPoints.question: Which insects are safest for students to observe in our area?
decisionPoints.guidance: If bees and butterflies present: Focus on beneficial pollinators from safe distance. If limited insects: Use photos and videos to supplement any live observations.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on beneficial insects or observe all spring insects?
decisionPoints.guidance: If teaching opportunity: Emphasize helpful insects like bees and butterflies. If general observation: Look at variety but emphasize beneficial roles.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for discussions about insect-flower relationships?
decisionPoints.guidance: If making connections: Explain how insects visit flowers for food. If complex: Focus on simple observation of insects near flowers.

lessons.opening: Connecting flowers to insects (8 min): Review beautiful spring flowers from Lesson 11. Ask students if they've noticed any small flying creatures near flowers. Introduce concept: insects love flowers! Show pictures of bees, butterflies, and other spring insects.
lessons.mainActivity: Spring insect observation (27 min): Outdoor insect investigation focusing on beneficial insects and their relationship with flowers. Students observe insects from safe distance using insect observation sheets. Practice vocabulary: 'Les insectes visitent les fleurs.' Look for bees on flowers, butterflies flying around, other insects in spring environment. Create class chart showing which insects visit which flowers. Discuss why insects like flowers (nectar for food) and how this helps plants (insects carry pollen). Simple movement activity: students act as flowers, others as visiting insects.
lessons.closing: Insect-flower connection understanding (10 min): Students share their insect observations and demonstrate insect movements they saw. Review how insects and flowers help each other. End with pollination dance: flower students stand still, insect students visit flowers and 'collect nectar.'
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If students are afraid of insects: Emphasize observation from distance and helpful role of insects. If few insects visible: Use videos or pictures and discuss what insects might be doing. If insects become aggressive: Move to different location or indoor observation.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand why they see bees and butterflies around flowers in their gardens and neighborhoods
lessons.visualSupports: Beneficial insect identification cards, insect movement demonstrations, flower-insect connection pictures, safety observation guidelines

lessons.title: Notre jardin de printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will plan and start a spring garden to observe plant growth throughout the season

decisionPoints.question: What plants are most appropriate for our classroom spring garden?
decisionPoints.guidance: If outdoor space available: Plant easy vegetables like radishes or lettuce. If indoor only: Use herbs or fast-growing flowers in containers.

decisionPoints.question: Should we plant vegetables, flowers, or herbs?
decisionPoints.guidance: If curriculum connections desired: Mix vegetables for nutrition unit connections. If simple maintenance: Choose flowers for beauty and easy care.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for ongoing plant care responsibilities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If responsibility skills developing: Assign garden care teams with rotating duties. If need support: Teacher manages care with student observation and help.

lessons.opening: Culminating plant learning (8 min): Review all plant learning from previous lessons: seeds growing, plants needing warmth and sun, flowers appearing. Introduce exciting project: creating our own class spring garden! Show examples of spring gardens and discuss what we might grow.
lessons.mainActivity: Spring garden planning and planting (27 min): Collaborative garden creation project applying all spring plant learning. Students help choose what to plant, prepare soil, plant seeds or seedlings, and set up garden care system. Practice vocabulary: 'Nous créons notre jardin de printemps.' Each student has a role in garden setup. Create garden care calendar showing when to water, observe, and tend plants. Students make predictions about how garden will change over time. Set up garden observation journals for ongoing documentation.
lessons.closing: Garden commitment ceremony (10 min): Students make commitment to care for class garden throughout spring. Explain how garden will help us continue learning about spring plant growth. End with garden care pledge and movements showing different garden care activities.
materials: Seeds or seedlings appropriate for season
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If weather prevents outdoor planting: Create indoor container garden. If plants don't establish: Have backup plants ready. If student interest varies: Assign specific garden roles to maintain engagement.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students experience how families grow their own food and flowers in home gardens
lessons.visualSupports: Garden planning templates, plant care instruction cards, garden tool identification, growth prediction charts

lessons.title: Notre livre scientifique de printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will create a class science book documenting all their spring observations and discoveries

decisionPoints.question: What format works best for student spring science documentation?
decisionPoints.guidance: If writing skills developing: Focus on drawings with simple captions. If ready for more: Include student-dictated longer descriptions.

decisionPoints.question: Should we include drawings, photos, or written observations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comprehensive documentation desired: Mix drawings, photos, and writing. If simpler approach: Focus on student drawings with teacher-recorded observations.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for collaborative book creation activities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If collaboration skills strong: Students work together to organize and create book sections. If need structure: Teacher organizes with student contributions.

lessons.opening: Celebrating spring learning (8 min): Review all the amazing spring discoveries from Lessons 1-13. Show students their accumulated work: observation sheets, drawings, garden journals. Announce special project: creating a book about our spring science journey!
lessons.mainActivity: Spring science book creation (27 min): Collaborative documentation project synthesizing all spring learning into class book. Students organize their drawings, observations, and discoveries into book sections: spring signs, plant growth, animal activity, flowers and insects, our garden. Practice vocabulary: 'Nous documentons nos découvertes.' Students contribute pages showing their best spring observations with drawings and simple captions. Create book sections for: what we learned about spring weather, plant changes, animal behaviors, experiments we did. Students practice presenting their pages to classmates.
lessons.closing: Book completion celebration (10 min): Students share favorite pages from spring science book. Discuss how their book shows all the amazing things they learned about spring. Plan to share book with families or other classes. End with proud scientist celebration dance.
materials: All accumulated student work from previous lessons
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If students overwhelmed by organizing: Teacher pre-organizes materials by themes. If some students have little work: Pair with partners or focus on current contributions. If book creation too complex: Simplify to class poster or display format.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand how scientists document and share their discoveries to help others learn about nature
lessons.visualSupports: Book organization templates, example science books, documentation guidelines, celebration display ideas

lessons.title: Prédictions: que va-t-il se passer en été?
lessons.oneGoal: Students will use their spring observations to make scientific predictions about summer changes (extension)

decisionPoints.question: Which predictions can students reasonably make based on spring observations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If pattern recognition developing: Focus on logical extensions (warmer weather, more plant growth). If need support: Use guided prediction activities with choices.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on plant, animal, or weather predictions?
decisionPoints.guidance: If students interested in specific area: Follow their interest with deeper predictions. If need variety: Make predictions about all three areas studied.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for hypothesis-making based on evidence?
decisionPoints.guidance: If scientific thinking developing: Connect predictions to evidence from spring observations. If need simpler: Focus on 'what do you think will happen' questions.

lessons.opening: Transitioning to summer thinking (8 min): Review spring science book from Lesson 14. Ask students what they think will happen as spring continues into summer. Show calendar indicating progression of seasons. Introduce prediction concept with simple examples.
lessons.mainActivity: Summer prediction investigation (27 min): Extension activity using spring learning to predict summer changes. Students use their spring observations to make logical predictions about summer: Will it get even warmer? Will plants grow bigger? What will happen to our garden? Practice vocabulary: 'Je prédis qu'en été...' Create prediction charts for weather, plants, and animals based on spring patterns observed. Students draw pictures showing their summer predictions. Discuss what evidence from spring supports their predictions.
lessons.closing: Prediction sharing and planning (10 min): Students present their summer predictions with reasoning. Plan how they might test their predictions over the summer. End with future scientist excitement about continuing observations.
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If predictions unrealistic: Guide students back to evidence from spring observations. If students not engaged: Make it game-like with prediction contests. If too abstract: Focus on concrete changes they might observe.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students practice thinking like scientists by using evidence to predict future natural changes
lessons.visualSupports: Seasonal progression charts, prediction templates, evidence reference materials, future observation planning sheets

lessons.title: Printemps autour du monde
lessons.oneGoal: Students will explore how spring looks different in various climates and regions (extension)

decisionPoints.question: Which global spring examples are most accessible to Grade 1 students?
decisionPoints.guidance: If global awareness developing: Use photos from different countries showing spring variations. If need concrete: Compare with familiar places students might know.

decisionPoints.question: Should we use photos, videos, or maps to explore different regions?
decisionPoints.guidance: If visual learning strong: Focus on photos and videos of spring in different places. If need geographic concepts: Use simple maps with spring examples marked.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for climate comparison activities?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comparison skills developing: Contrast spring in warm vs. cool climates. If need simpler: Focus on similarities in spring changes worldwide.

lessons.opening: Expanding spring perspective (8 min): Review local spring observations from all previous lessons. Introduce concept: spring happens all around the world, but looks different in different places! Show globe and indicate different locations where spring occurs.
lessons.mainActivity: World spring exploration (27 min): Extension investigation of global spring variations using photos, videos, and simple maps. Students observe photos of spring in different climates: desert spring, tropical spring, arctic spring, mountain spring. Practice vocabulary: 'Le printemps est différent partout dans le monde.' Compare similarities and differences to local spring observations. Create world spring display showing how spring plants, animals, and weather vary globally. Students choose favorite global spring example to draw and explain.
lessons.closing: Global spring appreciation (10 min): Students share their favorite examples of spring around the world. Discuss similarities in spring changes everywhere (warming, growing, animal activity). End with world spring celebration representing different global spring examples.
materials: Photos of spring in different world regions
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If global concept too abstract: Focus on comparing spring in nearby different places first. If overwhelmed by variety: Choose 2-3 clear contrasting examples. If materials limited: Use books or internet resources for global spring photos.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students understand that children around the world experience spring differently but share similar natural changes
lessons.visualSupports: World spring photo collection, climate comparison charts, global map with spring indicators, cultural spring celebration images

lessons.title: Expérience: créer des conditions de printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will design experiments to recreate spring conditions and observe their effects (extension)

decisionPoints.question: What spring conditions can students safely recreate in classroom experiments?
decisionPoints.guidance: If experimental skills developing: Set up controlled warmth and light experiments. If need simpler: Focus on one variable like warmth or light on plant growth.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on warmth, light, or water changes?
decisionPoints.guidance: If students engaged with plant experiments: Test effects of different spring conditions on plant growth. If need variety: Try multiple condition experiments with different materials.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for experiment design rather than just following procedures?
decisionPoints.guidance: If scientific method understood: Guide students to design their own spring condition tests. If need structure: Provide experiment templates they can modify.

lessons.opening: Connecting to spring conditions (8 min): Review all spring conditions learned: warmth, longer light, more water from spring rains. Challenge students: Can we create spring conditions inside to see what happens?
lessons.mainActivity: Spring conditions experiment design (27 min): Advanced extension activity where students design experiments to test spring conditions. Students set up controlled experiments: plants with extra warmth vs. normal temperature, plants with extra light vs. normal light, plants with spring-like watering vs. winter-like watering. Practice vocabulary: 'Nous créons des expériences.' Students make predictions about results and set up observation schedules. Create experiment recording sheets to track changes over time. Discuss experimental design concepts appropriate for Grade 1.
lessons.closing: Experiment launch celebration (10 min): Students explain their experiment designs and predictions. Plan ongoing observation schedule. End with scientist excitement about discovering results.
materials: Additional plants or seeds for experiments
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If experiments too complex: Simplify to teacher-designed experiments with student predictions. If materials insufficient: Use one class experiment with student input on design. If confusion about variables: Focus on one clear experimental comparison.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students learn how scientists use controlled experiments to understand how environmental conditions affect living things
lessons.visualSupports: Experiment design templates, variable identification cards, prediction recording sheets, scientific method visual guides

lessons.title: Le printemps et les humains
lessons.oneGoal: Students will investigate how humans adapt their behaviors and activities for spring changes (extension)

decisionPoints.question: Which human spring adaptations are most visible to students?
decisionPoints.guidance: If observational skills strong: Focus on clothing changes, activity changes, and food changes they can observe. If need concrete: Start with obvious changes like clothing and outdoor play.

decisionPoints.question: Should we focus on clothing, activities, or food changes?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comprehensive understanding desired: Cover all three adaptation areas. If need focus: Choose area most relevant to students' experiences.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for comparing human and animal spring behaviors?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comparison skills developed: Compare human adaptations to animal behaviors studied earlier. If complex: Focus on human adaptations first, make connections later.

lessons.opening: Connecting to human behavior (8 min): Review animal spring behaviors from previous lessons. Ask students how people change their behavior in spring too. Start with obvious examples like clothing and outdoor activities.
lessons.mainActivity: Human spring adaptation investigation (27 min): Extension exploration of how humans respond to spring changes through behavioral adaptations. Students investigate human spring changes: lighter clothing, more outdoor activities, spring cleaning, gardening, different foods. Practice vocabulary: 'Les humains s'adaptent au printemps.' Compare human and animal spring behaviors: both become more active, both prepare homes (animals build nests, humans do spring cleaning), both take advantage of better weather. Create comparison chart showing human vs. animal spring adaptations. Students interview each other about family spring traditions and changes.
lessons.closing: Human-animal spring connection (10 min): Students share family spring traditions and compare to animal behaviors. Celebrate similarities between human and animal responses to spring. End with adaptation movement showing both human and animal spring activities.
materials: Interview sheets for family spring traditions
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If comparison too abstract: Focus on concrete human spring changes first. If cultural variations cause confusion: Celebrate different family spring traditions. If time runs short: Focus on most obvious adaptations like clothing and activities.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students recognize that their families adapt to spring just like animals do, changing activities and behaviors for the season
lessons.visualSupports: Human spring adaptation cards, family activity pictures, comparison chart templates, cultural spring tradition examples

lessons.title: Présentation scientifique de printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will present their spring science discoveries to others using scientific language and evidence (extension)

decisionPoints.question: What format best allows students to share their spring learning?
decisionPoints.guidance: If presentation skills developing: Use show-and-tell format with science evidence. If need support: Provide presentation templates or partner presentations.

decisionPoints.question: Should presentations focus on individual discoveries or group findings?
decisionPoints.guidance: If individual confidence building desired: Each student presents one spring discovery. If collaborative learning emphasized: Groups present different spring topics.

decisionPoints.question: Are students ready for answering questions about their observations?
decisionPoints.guidance: If communication skills strong: Encourage audience questions and student responses. If need structure: Provide question prompts for audience to use.

lessons.opening: Preparing to share learning (8 min): Review all spring science learning from throughout the unit. Explain that scientists share their discoveries with others. Today students become spring science presenters!
lessons.mainActivity: Spring science presentation preparation and delivery (27 min): Culminating extension activity where students prepare and deliver presentations about spring science learning. Students choose their best spring discovery to share: plant growth experiments, animal observations, weather measurements, garden progress, or other spring learning. Practice vocabulary: 'Je présente mes découvertes scientifiques.' Students prepare simple presentations using drawings, photos, or actual materials as evidence. Practice presenting to small groups first, then to whole class. Include question and answer sessions after each presentation.
lessons.closing: Presentation celebration (10 min): Celebrate all student presentations and scientific communication growth. Discuss what made presentations effective. End with proud scientist applause for everyone's spring discoveries.
materials: All accumulated student work from unit
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If students nervous about presenting: Start with partner sharing or small groups. If presentations too long: Set time limits and focus on one key discovery. If audience restless: Include interactive elements or movement breaks.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students practice important communication skills that scientists use to share discoveries with other people
lessons.visualSupports: Presentation template guides, scientific evidence examples, communication skill visual reminders, audience participation guidelines

lessons.title: Fête des petits scientifiques de printemps
lessons.oneGoal: Students will celebrate their spring science journey with families by sharing experiments and discoveries (extension)

decisionPoints.question: How can the celebration showcase each student's scientific growth?
decisionPoints.guidance: If comprehensive showcase desired: Include displays of student work, live demonstrations, and student presentations. If simpler format: Focus on science book sharing and garden tours.

decisionPoints.question: Should we include live plant demonstrations or displays of completed work?
decisionPoints.guidance: If active demonstration appeals: Include seed planting or plant growth demonstrations. If display focus preferred: Showcase science books, drawings, and garden progress photos.

decisionPoints.question: What activities best demonstrate student learning to families?
decisionPoints.guidance: If interactive experience desired: Include hands-on science stations families can experience. If presentation focus: Have students guide families through their learning journey.

lessons.opening: Celebration preparation (8 min): Review entire spring science journey with students. Explain that they will share their learning with families. Assign roles and practice celebration activities.
lessons.mainActivity: Spring science celebration event (27 min): Culminating extension celebration where students showcase spring science learning to families and community. Students lead families through learning stations: spring observation displays, plant growth demonstrations, garden tours, science book sharing, animal behavior explanations, weather measurement activities. Practice vocabulary: 'Nous célébrons nos découvertes scientifiques.' Students act as science guides explaining their discoveries to visitors. Include hands-on activities families can try together. Display all student work and accomplishments from the unit.
lessons.closing: Celebration wrap-up and reflection (10 min): Thank families for participating. Students reflect on their favorite spring science discoveries. End with group celebration of becoming spring scientists and commitment to continue observing nature.
materials: All student work from unit displayed
lessons.whenThingsGoWrong: If family participation limited: Adapt to classroom celebration with other classes as audience. If activities too complex: Focus on simple sharing and display viewing. If weather interferes: Adapt outdoor activities to indoor alternatives.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Students experience the joy of sharing scientific discoveries with their families and build community connections around learning
lessons.visualSupports: Celebration activity station signs, student guide role cards, family participation guidelines, science learning showcase displays
